data.title: Trump Waives Russia Energy Tariffs, Sanctions A Week After Diesel Deal As Crude Oil Prices Soar To A 5-Month High
data.description:
Key points:
  • The Graham Act, signed into law on Sept. 18, authorized sanctions, restrictions and duties targeting Russia and certain foreign persons and countries.
  • The law also allows the president to waive those measures if he certifies to Congress that doing so is in the national interest of the U.S.
  • Trump’s Oct. 16 executive order invokes that authority, stating that he has submitted the required certification and report to Congress.

President Donald Trump has waived the application of new Russia-related sanctions and tariffs authorized under the recently enacted Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act.

The waiver, issued Friday, comes less than a month after Trump signed the Graham Act into law and about a week after the administration’s diesel deal with Russia.

Trump Waives New Russia Tariffs

The Graham Act, signed into law on Sept. 18, authorized sanctions, restrictions and duties targeting Russia and certain foreign persons and countries. The law also allows the president to waive those measures if he certifies to Congress that doing so is in the national interest of the U.S.

Trump’s Oct. 16 executive order invokes that authority, stating that he has submitted the required certification and report to Congress. The president waived the application of duties provided under key sections of the Graham Act, as well as several sanctions and restrictions targeting foreign persons.

However, the order leaves a framework in place for potentially steep tariffs on Russian goods and countries that continue to buy Russian energy or facilitate sanctions evasion.

The waiver will remain in effect until Trump or the Secretary of State, in consultation with other senior officials, determines that further action is appropriate.

Existing Russia-related sanctions imposed under earlier executive orders have been kept in place.

Trump Sets Up Sweeping Russia Tariff Structure

Trump’s executive order also laid out a sweeping tariff structure that could be activated against Russia and countries involved in Russian energy trade.

The order calls for a 500% ad valorem duty on goods from Russia, subject to exceptions in the Graham Act and the waivers issued by Trump.

It also provides for an additional 100% tariff on goods from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil and natural gas if those countries knowingly make new purchases of Russian-origin crude or natural gas on or after Oct. 18.

The order directs the U.S. Trade Representative, working with the State, Treasury and Energy departments, to monitor Russian oil and gas purchases and sanctions evasion and regularly report developments to Trump.

Crude Oil Prices Hit Five-Month High

Crude oil prices rose last week, with the U.S. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures expiring in November rising 10.88% to $101.84 a barrel after a 0.81% gain the week before. Brent crude futures expiring in December rose 4.91% this week, hovering around $109.69 a barrel after a 2.42% increase the week before.

The United States Oil Fund ETF (USO) rose about 3% on Friday, while the ProShares Ultra Bloomberg Crude Oil ETF (UCO) gained more than 4%.

During the after-hours session on Friday, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), which tracks the S&P 500 index, fell 0.26%; the Invesco QQQ Trust ETF (QQQ) edged lower by 0.27%; and the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) declined 0.21%. Retail sentiment on Stocktwits toward the S&P 500 ETF was in the ‘bearish’ territory at the time of writing.

data.title: India bars sugarcane juice, syrup-based ethanol in 2026-27 tender; OMCs seek 1,100 crore litres
data.description:
India has barred oil marketing companies (OMCs) from procuring ethanol made from sugarcane juice, sugar, sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses for the 2026-27 ethanol supply year, with the government directing that sugar diversion for ethanol be reduced to zero.

The restriction is set out in a quantity bid tender dated October 16, issued by five state-run oil companies for the supply of around 1,100 crore litres of denatured anhydrous ethanol between November 1, 2026, and October 31, 2027.

The tender allows procurement from C-heavy molasses, damaged food grains, surplus rice sourced from the Food Corporation of India (FCI), maize and other eligible feedstocks under the National Policy on Biofuels. The move comes amid concerns over domestic sugar availability and prices.

The participating companies are Indian Oil Corporation, Bharat Petroleum Corporation, Hindustan Petroleum Corporation, Mangalore Refinery and Petrochemicals and Numaligarh Refinery.

Corn, rice and damaged food grains among eligible feedstocks

The tender specifies different procurement rates depending on the feedstock. Ethanol made from maize has a basic rate of ₹66.07 per litre, with an additional incentive of ₹2.79 per litre, excluding Goods and Services Tax (GST).

The basic procurement rate for ethanol made from damaged food grains is ₹64 per litre, while surplus rice procured from FCI carries a rate of ₹60.32 per litre. Ethanol made from C-heavy molasses has a basic rate of ₹57.97 per litre.

Transportation charges and applicable GST are payable over and above the basic rates. Ethanol made from other eligible feedstocks under the National Policy on Biofuels will be procured at the lowest prevailing rate under the tender.

The tender covers four supply quarters, running from November 2026 to January 2027, February to April 2027, May to July 2027, and August to October 2027. However, offers for ethanol made from surplus FCI rice will not be accepted for the fourth quarter.

Allocations subject to pending court proceedings

The tender also states that ethanol allocations under the first quarter of the 2026-27 supply year will remain subject to the outcome of pending legal proceedings concerning the OMCs’ ethanol allocation methodology.

The companies have reserved the right to revise, reduce, withdraw or cancel allocations in line with court orders, without liability for compensation to suppliers.

The tender requires suppliers to offer ethanol produced from eligible indigenous feedstocks at their own registered or approved distilleries. Trading or sourcing ethanol from third parties for onward supply to the OMCs is not permitted.

The restrictions apply to procurement under this tender for the 2026-27 supply year, which begins on November 1.

data.title: Greenpeace activists occupy Woodside gas project unit off Western Australia
data.description:
Greenpeace said on Saturday activists occupied a floating production unit at Woodside's $12.5 billion Scarborough gas project off the coast of Western Australia state.

  • Four activists scaled the unit and displayed banners with message "Stop Woodside’s Dirty Gas. Save Scott Reef", the environmental advocacy group said on its website. The protest temporarily shut down operations at the semi-submersible unit, Greenpeace said.

  • Greenpeace is among environmental groups concerned about the project's potential impact on Scott Reef, a coral system and foraging area for the endangered pygmy blue whale located about 390 km (242 miles) off the state's northwest coast.

  • Woodside in a statement said it was "responding to an incident involving individuals who have gained unlawful access to the Scarborough floating production unit".

  • "Our immediate focus is on managing the situation safely and minimising risk to the individuals involved and our workforce," a Woodside spokesperson said.

  • Australian Border Force said it was aware of protest activity off the Western Australian coast and was working with federal and state agencies in response.

  • Woodside says it has conducted extensive environmental consultation on the project since 2018.

data.title: ECB's Rehn says staying vigilant to risk of second-round inflation effects
data.description:
European Central Bank policymaker Olli Rehn said on Saturday that policymakers would stay vigilant to the risk of second-round inflation effects from higher energy prices as they might creep in quietly.

"There is no sign of second-round effects, but we will stay vigilant because they might creep in quietly," the Finnish central bank chief said at an event in Bangkok.

data.title: Strong dollar, weak hand for Trump before midterms: McGeever
data.description:
By Jamie McGeever

With the US midterm elections weeks away, a surging dollar is exposing a central contradiction in President Donald Trump's economic agenda: currency markets are delivering the opposite of what his administration wants.

Trump's economic record in the first two years of his second term is being heavily scrutinized. Polls show voters' approval of his handling of the economy has rarely been lower. That goes a long way toward explaining why betting markets point to his Republican Party losing control of the House of Representatives, and perhaps even the Senate, on November 3.

Yet if there's any truth to the market adage that a country's currency is a reflection of the world's confidence in its economy, Trump should be going into the upcoming vote brimming with confidence. The dollar has been rising steadily, recently hitting its strongest level in 18 months against major peers.

But a strong and appreciating exchange rate is the last thing Trump wants. His administration's economic and trade policies are aiming to revive US manufacturing, make American exports great again and shrink the trade deficit. A strengthening currency won't help with any of that.

WRONG DIRECTION

One might expect the dollar to be under pressure, especially given that the US trade balance has not narrowed according to the administration's plan. Imports have exploded to record levels, largely driven by US companies hoovering up the chips, equipment and goods needed for the AI build-out, and the country's trade deficit is widening. It was 2.7% of gross domestic product earlier this year — one of the smallest readings of the century — but it could be headed for 4% of GDP next year, according to Dean Maki at hedge fund Point72.

But the dollar is not weakening. It did during Trump's first year back in the Oval Office, amid concerns about "dollar debasement" and a "sell America" mentality among foreign investors fostered by Trump's tariffs, but that has since gone into reverse.

Why? Because exchange rates are relative, and the greenback currently appears to be the proverbial "cleanest dirty shirt." While the US is suffering from acute debt and deficit concerns, so are other developed countries, most notably France. Investors fear that Paris is unwilling to take the politically unpalatable steps to get its budget under control and are thus slamming the euro .

Similarly, worries that higher interest rates will make it nearly impossible for Japan to service its enormous debt load have anchored the yen near its recent historical lows.

In short, the dollar is "winning" as much by default as it is benefiting from the flood of global capital chasing the US AI dream.

This is not what the White House had in mind.

Trump and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent clearly want a weaker dollar, even if decades of a quasi-official "strong dollar" policy at the White House — dating back to the days of former Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin in the 1990s — make it challenging for them to say so outright.

The Trump administration's views on the US currency were flagged almost exactly two years ago in "A User’s Guide to Restructuring the Global Trading System," a paper by Stephen Miran, then a senior strategist at hedge fund Hudson Bay Capital Management.

Miran went on to serve as chairman of the Council of Economic Advisers under Trump, who later appointed him as a Federal Reserve governor for a short spell. He has since returned to HBC, but his 41-page manual still appears to serve as a broad framework for the administration's trade, currency and economic policy.

The blueprint has come to be known as the "Mar-a-Lago Accord," in a nod to the famous 1985 "Plaza Accord," under which the world's leading economic powers agreed to devalue the dollar.

Echoing Trump's decades-long view, Miran wrote that "deep unhappiness with the prevailing economic order is rooted in persistent overvaluation of the dollar ... (which) makes US exports less competitive, US imports cheaper, and handicaps American manufacturing."

He has a point. At the time of Trump's inauguration in January last year, the dollar's broad, real effective exchange rate was the strongest in over 30 years.

Miran argues that the global trade and financial systems can be rewired to America's benefit, but the path "is narrow, and will require careful planning, precise execution, and attention to steps to minimize adverse consequences."

Americans casting their midterm election votes on November 3 may not have the patience for this. While the US economy continues to grow at a healthy pace and unemployment remains low, households are feeling the adverse economic consequences of Trump's policies over the past two years.

Tariffs have raised the cost of imported goods, according to a recent New York Fed study, and the US war with Iran, launched in February, has led to soaring energy costs, most notably record-high diesel prices at the pump. As a consequence, inflation remains elevated, bond yields are the highest in a quarter of a century, and real wages are now falling.

Given all this, the big question is whether the American public will give the Trump administration the space to try to turn the dollar's tide.

A FAREWELL TO MULTILATERALISM

Efforts to reverse the dollar's march higher will be challenging, to put it mildly. History suggests that what's needed is multilateral, globally coordinated action, but that is the antithesis of Trump's "America First" worldview.

Piecemeal and bilateral actions, like the Treasury's recent intervention with Japan to support the yen , are likely too small to have any lasting impact.

Further interventions cannot be ruled out if the dollar continues to strengthen.

For example, when writing about the yen, Stephen Jen, CEO of Eurizon SLJ Asset Management, recently argued that a series of targeted, surprise "mini" interventions could chip away at the dollar without triggering an avalanche of depreciation, helping the Trump administration meet its foreign exchange and wider goals over time.

"The Trump Administration ... wants to find ways to guide the dollar lower. This is needed because, in order for the US to attain economic security, it needs to reclaim a certain level of manufacturing self-sufficiency. To do that, a weaker dollar would be necessary. The challenge, of course, is to guide the dollar lower without spooking the capital markets," Jen wrote in May.

Much will depend on the frequency and size of such moves. Official action to weaken the dollar against major currencies is rare. Before this year's yen intervention, the last time US and Japanese authorities coordinated to sell dollars against the yen was in 1998. The Fed intervened with the European Central Bank and other authorities to support the euro, but that was back in late 2000, just after the single currency's launch.

Since the era of free-floating exchange rates began in the early 1970s, when President Richard Nixon took the US off the gold standard, there have only been two truly global efforts to force a change in the dollar's broad value. Both were in the 1980s: the Plaza Accord in 1985 to lower what was an extremely elevated dollar, and the Louvre Accord in 1987 to essentially take the sting out of Plaza.

These accords were products of their time. The dollar is nowhere near as strong as it was back then, and that was an era when multilateral cooperation was still in vogue.

As the country looks set to enter the final two years of the Trump era, the dollar's relative strength could say much about how much of his economic agenda he has been able to achieve since first entering the White House almost 10 years ago.

(The opinions expressed here are those of the author, a columnist for Reuters)

Enjoying this column? Check out Reuters Open Interest (ROI), your essential new source for global financial commentary. Follow ROI on LinkedIn, and X.

And listen to the Morning Bid daily podcast on Apple, Spotify, or the Reuters app. Subscribe to hear Reuters journalists discuss the biggest news in markets and finance seven days a week.

data.title: Trump Denies Ordering Starlink Curbs in Ukraine, Says ‘It Wasn’t Me and I Don’t Think It Was Elon’ as Zelenskyy Warns Slower Speeds Put Lives at Risk
data.description:
President Donald Trump has denied ordering restrictions on Space Exploration Technologies Corp.’s satellite connectivity in Ukraine, as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says reduced speeds disrupted drone interceptions and other military operations.

Trump Denies Role in Starlink Restrictions

Speaking to reporters Friday, Trump rejected suggestions that he had directed the restrictions affecting Ukraine’s military access to Starlink and Starshield services, CNBC reported.

"I don’t know if it was anybody because it wasn’t me and I don’t think it was Elon," Trump said, adding that, to his knowledge, the service remained as it had been.

Ukrainian officials said earlier this week that the restrictions disrupted military operations without prior warning. Starshield is a military-focused satellite communications service that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk says the U.S. government owns and controls.

Musk pointed to Washington’s authority over the system, while Reuters reported, citing U.S. officials, that the White House made the decision to limit Starshield connectivity. The report did not identify who issued the order.

The Telegraph separately reported that Musk had approached Trump about slowing Starlink in Ukraine, alleging that both played a role in the restrictions.

SpaceX did not immediately respond to Benzinga’s request for comment.

Read Also: Trump’s $330 Million White House Ballroom Donor List Reveals Nvidia, Apple and Google Among Top Tech Contributors: Report

Zelenskyy Says Speed Cuts Hampered Drone Interceptions

Zelenskyy said Ukraine does not use Starlink for attacks inside Russia but relies on the technology to intercept Russian attack drones targeting civilians.

"Starlink wasn’t turned off — its speed was reduced," Zelenskyy said on X, explaining that the slowdown prevented Ukrainian forces from intercepting some jet-powered Shahed drones.

"We couldn’t use a tool that helps protect people. That’s very painful and frustrating," he added.

Zelenskyy also said the restrictions affected Ukrainian strikes against military targets in Russian-occupied territories and drone deliveries of food and water to troops stationed on the front lines.

He said connectivity had not fully returned to its previous performance levels, although restoration efforts were underway.

data.title: IDBI Bank sale: Legitimate employee concerns addressed, says MoS, Finance
data.description:
Legitimate concerns of the existing employees and other stakeholders of IDBI Bank have been suitably addressed through appropriate provisions made in the Share Purchase Agreement, according to Pankaj Chaudhary, Minister of State for Finance.

In a reply to an un-starred question in the Lok Sabha by Thamizhachi Thangapandian, the minister said Preliminary Information Memorandum for inviting Expression of Interest (EoI) from potential bidders was published on October 7, 2022. In response, multiple EOIs were received, due diligence of which is being undertaken after security clearance by Ministry of Home Affairs and ‘fit and proper ‘evaluation by the Reserve Bank of India.

Issues raised in House

The original question in the House pertained to current status of privatisation; whether specific assessments were done by Government to evaluate potential impact on officers of the bank; whether Government has any plans to discuss implications of the proposed privatisation with employees and their representatives.

Big lie, says United Forum

Meanwhile, the United Forum of IDBI Officers and Employees expressed shock over the statement by Arunish Chawla, Secretary, Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM), that it had discussed the disinvestment with employee associations. “We condemn the statement that DIPAM discussed the matter with representatives of the United Forum, the largest employee forum with 11,900 officers and 400 workmen employees as members. The United Forum was never consulted while preparing or finalising the draft of Share Purchase Agreement nor was its draft shared. The statement of Secretary, DIPAM, is a big lie,” it said

Dharnas, strike held

“We sat in dharna at Jantar Mantar, Delhi, on seven occasions opposing the proposed sale of the bank to private/foreign players. A memorandum was submitted to Secretary, DIPAM, opposing the proposed sale that went against interests of the nation as well as employees,” said Devidas Tuljapurkar, Convenor and Vithal Koteswara Rao and Ratnakar Wankhade, Joint Convenors, of the United Forum.

A one day nation-wide strike was observed on August 11, 2025. Several conciliation meetings were conducted before Assistant Labour Commissioner (Central), Mumbai, and Deputy Chief Labour Commissioner (Central), Mumbai, in 2025 and 2026. “DIPAM officials never discussed the matter with us; rather replied every time to Labour Commissioners that the strategic disinvestment is a policy decision of Government of India and is a confidential process,” they said.

Confidential process

Earlier last month, a senior DIPAM official wrote to Assistant Labour Commissioner-C (III), Mumbai, that the “strategic disinvestment is a confidential process, and contains price sensitive information akin to any sale and purchase transaction of a listed company that is required by regulation to be kept confidential. Any disclosure of terms of disinvestment would not only vitiate transparency and confidentiality of the bidding process but also be a breach by Government of confidentiality regulations and jeopardise disinvestment process altogether.“

The DIPAM observed that invoking of conciliation process amounts to no more than case of ‘forum-shopping,’ with the Supreme Court yet to decide on a similar plea and another one pending with Mumbai High Court.

data.title: Can the Russia Sanctions Bill waiver by Donald Trump bring more relief to Indian markets?
data.description:
US President Donald Trump’s decision to waive new sanctions and tariffs under America’s Russia sanctions law could provide some relief to Indian markets by removing an immediate source of uncertainty over the country’s purchases of Russian oil.

The Sensex and Nifty recorded their biggest weekly gains since the first week of April 2026, supported by a strong rebound in IT stocks. However, with crude prices surging amid escalating geopolitical tensions and Brent briefly crossing $110 a barrel on Friday, October 16, the outlook for equities remains closely tied to energy prices and global risk sentiment.

Trump, in an executive order dated October 16, waived the sanctions, restrictions and duties provided for under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, citing US national interests. The law had envisaged a 100% increase in duties on goods from the five largest importers of Russian-origin crude oil and natural gas if they knowingly made new purchases from October 18, subject to specified exceptions.

India, a major buyer of Russian crude, had faced potential exposure to the proposed tariffs. The waiver removes the immediate threat of these additional duties under the law while it remains in force, although it does not exempt India from other existing US tariffs or sanctions.

IT stocks lead recovery as AI concerns ease

Friday's gains extended the benchmark indices’ winning streak to a second consecutive week, taking their weekly advances to the highest level since the first week of April.

IT stocks were among the strongest drivers of the recovery, with Nifty IT index emerging as the best-performing sector last week. It rose nearly 12% to record its biggest weekly gain in 18 years. The index gained another 4% on Friday to close at 31,924, its highest level in eight months.

The rally added nearly $30 billion to the combined market capitalisation of the top 10 Indian IT companies during the week. Tata Consultancy Services accounted for $13.3 billion of the increase, while Infosys added around $7 billion and HCL Technologies saw its market value rise by $5.3 billion.

The rebound followed better-than-expected results from Indian software companies and a pullback in global AI-related stocks, helping revive investor confidence in the domestic IT sector. The rally also came after the Nifty IT index had been the worst-performing sectoral gauge this year until Wednesday.

The gains in IT stocks have helped lift the broader market, although the performance has been uneven across sectors. The Nifty FMCG index fell nearly 1% over the week, while the midcap index declined 67 points to close at 59,130 on Friday. The Bank Nifty ended marginally higher at 55,844.

Veteran investor and BSE member Ramesh Damani said: “I think we are witnessing the early stages of a major rotation in equity markets. The AI-led boom, which has largely overlooked India over the past few years, is now beginning to lose steam amid higher interest rates, stretched valuations and excessive exuberance.”

Crude prices remain a key risk

Despite the potential relief from the US waiver, the sharp rise in crude prices remains a concern for India, which depends heavily on imports to meet its oil requirements.

Brent crude crossed $110 a barrel on Friday for the first time since May before closing at $109.86. US benchmark West Texas Intermediate (WTI) settled above $101 a barrel, taking its weekly gain to around 10%. Brent rose more than 5% over the week.

Prices climbed as Iran escalated attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, Yemen’s Houthi rebels continued attacks affecting Saudi Arabia, and Ukraine vowed to continue targeting Russian energy infrastructure.

The conflict has raised concerns over the security of energy supplies and shipping routes. Although Russian crude exports have remained above recent lows, shipments for the week ended Wednesday stood at 9.4 million barrels per day, around 70% of pre-war levels, according to energy research firm Kpler.

data.title: Bitcoin ETFs post $82.39 million in net outflows as Ethereum funds shed $69.68 million
data.description:
US spot Bitcoin ETFs lost $82.39 million in net outflows on October 16. Their Ethereum counterparts had no better luck. They gave up $69.68 million the same day.

Combined, the two product groups saw roughly $152 million leave in one session.

The bigger picture is the monthly tally. Bitcoin ETFs had run up roughly $535 million in net outflows for October through mid-month. That reverses September, when the funds pulled in about $2.6 billion of fresh money.

Bitcoin ETF trading volume topped $7.5 billion in the week ending October 16. Net selling over the past week came to only about $145 million.

Not every count of the day matched. Alternative tallies put Bitcoin's daily outflow as low as $10.6 million, with Fidelity's FBTC leading the redemptions. Reporting differences between data sources are common with ETF flows, which settle and get compiled on different schedules.

Despite the recent selling, the Bitcoin ETF complex remains enormous. Total assets are estimated at around $105 to $106 billion. The funds collectively hold more than 1.27 million BTC.

Measured against those assets, the $82.39 million outflow is less than a tenth of one percent.

BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust, ticker IBIT, is the largest Bitcoin ETF by assets. Fidelity's FBTC and Grayscale's GBTC round out the most closely watched names. Grayscale's fund has a longer history than most, having converted from a closed-end trust into a spot ETF.

Ethereum ETFs are a smaller pond. They hold approximately $15 billion in total assets. That makes the $69.68 million daily outflow proportionally heavier than Bitcoin's, even though the dollar figure is lower.

Spot Bitcoin ETFs launched in the US in January 2024. Since then, cumulative net inflows have totaled roughly $57 billion.

Against that backdrop, October's roughly $535 million in outflows amounts to less than 1% of everything that has flowed in since launch.

Bitcoin is trading near $82,000. Ethereum sits between $2,400 and $2,500.

More than $7.5 billion in weekly trading against about $145 million in net selling suggests engagement has not disappeared. It has turned cautious.

The simultaneous outflows from both Bitcoin and Ethereum funds point toward a broader risk-off posture rather than a view on one specific asset.

For Ethereum, with a much smaller asset base of approximately $15 billion, sustained outflows of this size would take a bigger proportional bite than equivalent dollar outflows from Bitcoin ETFs.

The spread between an $82.39 million outflow and a $10.6 million one is wide enough to change the tone of a day's coverage. For anyone trading on flow data, knowing which source you rely on is half the battle.

data.title: Houthi shelling in Taiz kills woman, wounds five civilians
data.description:
A woman was killed and five civilians, including another woman and a girl, were wounded in Houthi shelling and sniper fire in the Sabir al-Mawadim district, southeast of Taiz, according to the Taiz Human Rights Center as reported by Yemen's state news agency Saba. This incident is part of a pattern of increased hostilities in the region, where Iran-aligned Houthi forces have intensified their military activities. The ongoing conflict has led to a siege around Taiz, disrupting essential supplies and causing civilian casualties. The developments in Taiz are contributing to a broader context of escalating tensions between Houthi forces and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, with potential implications for the strategic city of Aden.

  • Recent shelling and sniper fire in Taiz appear consistent with heightened military activity by Houthi forces in the region.
  • Market pricing suggests that the likelihood of Houthi forces entering Aden has slightly increased, reflecting ongoing conflict escalation.
  • The probability of Houthi entry into Aden by December 31, 2026, remains higher than near-term projections, with the market pricing a 26% chance of this outcome.

Observers should monitor any further military advancements by Houthi forces, particularly movements towards strategic locations such as Lahj and Al-Anad Air Base. Confirmation of Houthi advances or significant military engagements could influence market expectations. Additionally, any diplomatic developments or changes in international military involvement might impact the likelihood of Houthi forces reaching Aden. The situation remains fluid, and markets are likely to respond to new information regarding military or political shifts in the region.

data.title: German minister seeks debt-brake exemption to sustain Ukraine aid
data.description:
By Maria Martinez

Germany's development minister is seeking an exemption from the country's debt brake, a constitutional limit on government borrowing, for Ukraine funding, arguing that much of Germany's civilian support for Ukraine comes from her ministry's budget.

"The Russian attacks are more severe than ever, leading to more deaths, more destruction, more suffering. But as budget cuts for development assistance continue, we simply will not be able to maintain our support for Ukraine at this level," Reem Alabali Radovan told Reuters on Friday, on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank meetings.

Funding for Ukraine in her ministry's budget amounts to about €330 million ($371 million) this year, down from €670 million in 2022 and €750 million in 2023.

"At this point, it is not a political decision; we just face massive cuts and it will no longer be possible," Alabali Radovan said. "This is especially hard as the money is wisely invested in Ukraine's and Europe's stability."

Alabali Radovan is a member of the Social Democrats, the junior partner of the governing coalition led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz's CDU.

Her proposal has the backing of Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, a member of the conservative CDU, but faces opposition from other members of the party who oppose further exceptions to borrowing rules beyond those already approved, such as for defence spending.

"I am already prioritising support for Ukraine, but there are many other crises and conflicts, too. And we work in the long term, which means large parts of our budget are already committed," Alabali Radovan said.

"That means the cuts hit crisis instruments above all, because – naturally – they work with flexible funds that are not yet pre-committed."

Alabali Radovan added that she supports Merz's call for other countries to contribute more.

"We are the strongest supporters, and I believe others can and should contribute more," she said.

($1 = 0.8887 euros)

data.title: Mongolia becomes new donor to World Bank's fund for poorest countries
data.description:
The World Bank Group said on Saturday that Mongolia has become a new donor to the International Development Association fund for the poorest countries, after previously spending nearly three decades as a recipient of IDA funding.

The development lender said that Mongolia's parliament approved a 4.8 billion tugrik ($1.3 million) contribution to the latest IDA funding round, marking a milestone in the country's development journey.

Since becoming a World Bank member country in 1991, Mongolia has received more than $1.62 billion in development financing, including IDA support for transport, rural development, health and education. Mongolia graduated from IDA support in July 2020, becoming a client of the World Bank's main lending arm for middle-income countries, the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development.

"Mongolia’s contribution to IDA21 marks an important milestone in our longstanding partnership with the World Bank and reflects our commitment to international solidarity," Mongolian Finance Minister Mendsaikhan Zagdjav said in a statement released by the World Bank.

"Having benefited firsthand from IDA’s support, we recognize the vital role of concessional financing in helping countries reduce poverty, build resilience, and expand opportunities. As we continue to advance Mongolia's own development priorities, we are proud to support other countries in pursuing theirs."

data.title: The week in charts: Jio's mega debut, deferred UPI charges, IDBI bank stake sale
data.description:
New Delhi, Oct. 17 -- From Jio Platforms preparing for what could be India's largest IPO to the deferment of charges on select UPI transactions, the week saw key developments across markets and banking.

The rupee gained against the dollar after a series of Reserve Bank of India measures, while the Union cabinet cleared the sale of a majority stake in IDBI Bank to Fairfax Financial Holdings, marking the biggest privatization since Air India in 2022. Meanwhile, Australia strengthened its lead in the ongoing World Test Championship cycle- here is this week's news in numbers.

The much-awaited initial public offering (IPO) of Jio Platforms, Mukesh Ambani's telecom business, will open on 21 October. At the upper end of its price band, the issue is set to raise Rs.30,200 crore, making it India's largest IPO, surpassing Hyundai Motor India's October 2024 offering.

Launched in 2016, Jio has grown into a major player in India's telecom sector, and the listing marks another milestone for Ambani's business. The shares will be listed on 28 October. At the upper end of its IPO price band, Jio Platforms' market capitalization would make it India's fourth-most-valuable listed company, after Reliance Industries, Bharti Airtel and HDFC Bank, based on market values as of Wednesday.

The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) has postponed the planned charge on select person-to-merchant (P2M) UPI transactions, citing the festive season.

UPI (unified payments interface) transactions have been free since the platform was launched in 2016. In September, the government announced a charge of 0.4% on P2M transactions above Rs.2,000, capped at Rs.300. The charge, which was earlier scheduled to take effect on 15 October, will now be implemented "immediately post Diwali", according to NPCI.

UPI transactions typically see their highest sequential growth in October, coinciding with the festive season, with March recording the next-highest growth.

Nearly four years after the government first announced plans to sell IDBI Bank, the Union cabinet on Wednesday cleared the sale of a 60.7% stake in the lender to Canada-based Fairfax Financial Holdings for Rs.52,877 crore. The stake is currently held by the government and the state-owned Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC).

The deal will be the latest foreign investment in India's financial sector, following Emirates NBD's investment in RBL Bank, Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corp.'s investment in Yes Bank and MUFG's investment in Shriram Finance.

It will also be the government's biggest privatisation since the sale of Air India to the Tata Group in 2022. Since then, the government has struggled to complete outright sales. Small stake sales, alongside the proposed IDBI Bank divestment, are putting 2026-27 on course to be the strongest year for disinvestment since 2017-18.

23%: The average forecast by five brokerages for growth in Nifty 50 companies' net profit in the September quarter, compared with 11% growth in the June quarter.

36.7 million sq ft: Net absorption of office space across eight major Indian cities in January-September, down 20% from a year earlier, according to Cushman & Wakefield.

Rs.3,191 crore: Net profit reported by SaaS company Zoho in 2024-25. This week, co-founder Sridhar Vembu said the company would not give salary hikes this year amid disruption from artificial intelligence (AI).

12%: Share of Indian consumers who reported being scammed in the previous 12 months, according to GSMA's India Consumer Scam Report 2026. Among scam victims, 86% took their cases to an organisation.

$276 million: Amount Elon Musk has spent on Republican midterm election efforts since July, making him the largest known donor in the 2026 US election cycle.

The rupee gained about 1.8% against the US dollar this week, following a series of foreign exchange measures announced by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) last week. It closed at Rs.95.03 to the dollar on 14 October.

The measures were aimed at easing immediate dollar demand and curbing positions in currency derivatives. Between 7 September and 8 October, the rupee had depreciated 2.5%. Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi this week, finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman said the RBI would seek to curb volatility in the rupee, which was under pressure from external factors, but would not attempt to fix its value.

The World Test Championship (WTC) 2025-27 cycle is underway, with Australia leading the standings after a recent 214-run win over South Africa in the first Test of their three-match series. Australia has won nine of its 11 Tests in the current cycle and lost two, earning about 82% of the points available.

South Africa is third with 60%, while India is fifth with 51.5%. The top two teams at the end of the cycle will meet in the final at The Oval in England in June 2027. South Africa's remaining fixtures include home series against Bangladesh and England and a tour of Sri Lanka.

India will tour New Zealand and host Australia, leaving it needing a strong run of wins and favourable results elsewhere to reach the final.

data.title: DHL Raises FY26 EBIT Outlook After Strong Q3 Performance
data.description:
BONN (dpa-AFX) - DHL Group, now officially known as DHL AG, raised its full-year 2026 EBIT outlook, citing continued earnings momentum, particularly in its Express division, and indications of a robust seasonal peak in the fourth quarter.

The company now expects reported group EBIT to exceed 7.0 billion euros, compared with its previous forecast of more than 6.5 billion euros.

DHL increased its outlook for DHL divisions EBIT to more than 6.4 billion euros from more than 5.9 billion euros previously. The outlook remains unchanged for Post & Parcel Germany, where EBIT is expected to exceed 900 million euros, and for Group Functions, which is forecast to post EBIT of around negative 400 million euros.

The revised guidance follows strong preliminary third-quarter results. DHL said group revenue rose more than 12% year over year to approximately 22.6 billion euros in the third quarter of 2026.

Preliminary group EBIT increased to about 1.71 billion euros from 1.48 billion euros a year earlier, representing growth of roughly 16%.

DHL is scheduled to publish its full third-quarter 2026 results on November 5, 2026.

DHL AG (DHLGY) shares closed up 1.73% at $33.00 on October 16.

data.title: Sunil Singhania makes a fresh entry in this defence stock
data.description:
New Delhi, Oct. 17 -- Building a successful stock portfolio requires a clear investment strategy, well-defined financial goals and a thorough understanding of market dynamics.

As you develop your own approach, you can also draw valuable lessons from the experience and investment philosophies of seasoned market veterans.

Studying their decisions can offer useful insights, but these must be balanced with your own financial objectives, risk appetite and investment horizon.

One such investor is Sunil Singhania, whose investment moves and portfolio choices attract considerable attention.

Sunil Singhania is the founder of Abakkus Asset Manager, an investment management company.

He has a track record of over two decades in equity markets. He played a significant role in building Reliance-Nippon MF into one of India's largest asset management companies (AMCs).

Sunil Singhania has picked up a stake in defence stock Bharat Earth Movers.

According to the latest shareholding pattern for Sept 2026, investor Sunil Singhania now holds a 1.1% stake in the company. His holding is now valued at Rs.1,769 million (m).

He held no stake in the company in the prior quarters.

While the reasons for the hike remain unclear, a few points may explain the decision.

Q1 FY27 has been a big improvement for BEML and the best first quarter the company has had in the last decade or so, with top-line growth of 29%.

This growth was led by a tremendous turnaround in the Rail and Metro segment, which grew by 178%. It was the first time that BEML hit a positive EBITDA ever and the overall loss has gone down by almost 50%.

Improving financials could be one reason Sunil Singhania picked a stake in the company.

The company has a strong order book of more than Rs.16000 crore. According to the management, BEML is looking at an opportunity size of Rs.35000 crore to Rs.40000 crore, mainly led by the Metro and Rail.

In the defence and mining space, BEML has L1 value of around Rs.900 crore worth of tenders.

The company also has a healthy export order book currently at around US$115 million and the management is optimistic it should end the year with an export order book of around US$200 million.

These may be some of the reasons Sunil Singhania picked a stake in the stock.

BEML's future performance will depend on its ability to convert its sizeable order book into timely execution, revenue growth and sustainable profitability.

The sharp improvement in the Rail and Metro segment is encouraging, but the company must show it can maintain this momentum in subsequent quarters.

Progress in defence, mining and exports could provide additional growth opportunities, while new orders may strengthen revenue visibility.

However, tender conversions, project delays, working-capital requirements and execution costs remain important factors to monitor.

In the past week, the BEML stock is up nearly 3%. However, in the last month, the share price has changed very little. In the past year, the share price has lost 5%.

The stock touched its 52-week high of Rs.2,275.75 on 24 October 2025 and its 52-week low of Rs.1,355 on 30 March 2026.

BEML Ltd is a government-owned engineering and manufacturing company established in May 1964. Headquartered in Bengaluru, it operates under the Ministry of Defence, with the Government of India holding a 54.03% stake.

The company manufactures a wide range of products across three business segments: Defence and Aerospace, Mining and Construction, and Rail and Metro. Its products include military vehicles, missile launchers, bulldozers, excavators, mining dump trucks, railway coaches, metro cars and trainsets. BEML has manufacturing facilities in Bengaluru, Kolar Gold Fields, Mysuru and Palakkad.

data.title: A $2,000,000,000,000 fund may lift a self-imposed ban on Western defence stocks; Details here
data.description:
Norway's $2.3 trillion sovereign wealth fund, the largest in the world, could soon end its self-imposed ban on investing in Western defence companies that has lasted years.

The fund currently has stakes in around 1.5% of the publicly listed companies globally, making it one of the biggest investors in the global stock market.

Last week, an independent Gjedrem committee submitted a review to Norway's Finance Ministry, which included a recommendation for a radical change to how the fund approaches defence investments. It argued that Norges Bank must be prepared for situations where conflicts escalate into war. The review was ordered in November 2025, after controversy broke out over some disinvestments from some Israeli and US-based firms.

Norges Bank has not invested in western defence companies for years as their current ethical rules prohibit them from making investments in companies such as Airbus, BAE Systems, Boeing, BWX Technologies and Lockheed Martin, as they contribute to the manufacturing of nuclear weapons.

It is not as if the fund does not invest in defence stocks at all. It does have a 2.3% stake in Germany's Rheinmetall, and a 1.5% stake in Leonardo, listed in Italy.

As per the Gjedrem Committee recommendation, although the nuclear weapons criteria should be retained, its scope could change.

The Fund is not to be invested in companies that produce nuclear weapons, unless the company is domiciled in a nuclear-weapon state under the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) that is allied with Norway. Several European and American companies that produce components for nuclear weapons can therefore be reincluded.

According to the recommendations, the fund should invest in companies producing weapons that Norway needs for its own defence, and also proposed to remove the requirement for arms manufacturers to be assessed for whether their products are being used by countries in accordance with international humanitarian laws.

Apart from the rising geopolitical risks, the committee believes that given the fund's capital and influence, it was time to reassess the ethical framework.

Norway's oil fund was set up in the 1990s to invest the windfall from the country's oil and gas industry. Investment decisions are made by Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM), which also holds stake in many Indian listed entities.

In September last year, controversy broke out after the NBIM ordered exiting positions in American machinery manufacturer Caterpillar and five other Israeli banks, which prompted the US state department to retort by saying that it is "very troubled" by the decision of the fund, which, as per them, was based on "illegitimate claims."

The committee also recommended that the Council of Ethics must continue to operate but no longer advise NBIM on taking action over ethical concerns.

Norway's Finance Ministry will now propose a new ethics framework in a white paper during spring, and Norway's parliament is expected to vote on the new proposed framework sometime in mid-2027. Till then, the current guidelines remain in place.

data.title: BOJ may need to tighten faster if inflation beats forecast, IMF says
data.description:
Key points:
  • IMF sees BOJ 'doing the right thing' in normalising policy
  • Japan 'fully committed' to floating exchange rate, IMF says
  • IMF analysis suggests yen moves since mid-2025 not driven by fundamentals
  • Japan must clarify means of funding for spending plans

By Leika Kihara

The Bank of Japan is "doing the right thing" by normalising monetary policy and may need to raise interest rates faster if inflation rises more than expected, a senior International Monetary Fund official told Reuters.

Japan must also clarify how it plans to fund its big spending plans and lay out a medium-term fiscal framework to ease market concerns about fiscal risks, said Krishna Srinivasan, director of the IMF's Asia and Pacific Department.

"I would say that they are doing the right thing at this point," Srinivasan said on the BOJ's efforts to lift its policy rate towards levels deemed neutral to the economy.

"If inflation rises faster than expected, you have to start tightening faster because you don't want inflation expectations to get un-anchored. It's data dependent," he said in an interview on Friday.

The remarks came ahead of the BOJ's key policy meeting later this month, when it could keep rates steady but drop hawkish hints that would reinforce dominant market expectations of a December hike.

Inflationary pressures from the Middle East conflict and brisk AI-demand were among key themes discussed by policymakers gathering for this week's annual IMF meetings in Bangkok.

BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda, who attended the IMF meetings, said on Friday the central bank will focus on anchoring underlying inflation around its 2% target and won't tolerate any overshoot, stressing anew its resolve to continue raising interest rates.

For Japan, a weak yen adds to factors pushing up inflation by boosting the cost of raw material imports.

Such mounting price pressures prodded the BOJ to raise rates to a 31-year high of 1.25% in September, following a hike in June. Many analysts expect another rate increase by year-end.

Japan also conducted a rare, coordinated intervention with the US on July 31 to prevent the currency's slide to near 40-year lows from destabilising financial markets.

In staff analysis included in its report on Asia's economy, the IMF said a big portion of yen moves since mid-2025 had little to do with fundamental factors such as yield differentials, and instead co-moved with speculative positions in yen futures.

"Japan has a deep foreign exchange market, so as a first line of defense, they have allowed the exchange rate to move," Srinivasan said.

"Bottom line, I would say that the Japanese authorities are fully committed to a freely floating exchange rate. I've had many discussions with them. So I don't doubt that at all," he said when asked if the recent yen intervention was justified.

FISCAL FRAMEWORK NEEDED

Rising global bond yields have also drawn attention at this week's IMF meetings as debt in advanced economies, including Japan, expanded after years of heavy spending.

Markets worry that Japan may add to its already huge debt pile with the administration's big spending plans and a two-year cut to the consumption tax from April next year.

Srinivasan said Japan has in fact seen fiscal consolidation proceed more than any other G7 country since the pandemic due in part to rising tax revenues.

"Markets are concerned about the fiscal risks because of the uncertainty" on how Japan would pay for the fresh spending and tax-cut plans, he said. "Japan also would benefit from having a medium-term fiscal framework."

data.title: IDBI Bank sale: Keep CCEA decision in abeyance pending independent inquiry, says EAS Sarma
data.description:
Former Secretary to government of India EAS Sarma has demanded that Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) decision on October 14 to disinvest government’s and LIC’s holdings in IDBI be kept in abeyance pending an independent inquiry.

The findings should be presented to Parliament, Sarma wrote in his latest letter to Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman. “I consider this decision to be ill-advised as it involves serious legal implications, gross undervaluation of IDBI’s assets, and a breach of assurance given by government,” he said in the letter shared with businessline.

Sold for a ‘pittance’

Sarma recalled he had raised ‘multiple concerns’ about disinvestment in his previous letter of August 4, citing a ‘highly opaque, non-competitive environment.’ But CCEA has since approved selection of ‘M/s 10955230 Canada Inc., whose parent entity is Fairfax Financial Holdings Ltd.,’ as the strategic buyer for IDBI’s disinvestment.

Purchase consideration is ₹52,878 crore for the acquisition of a 60.72 per cent stake in IDBI Bank Ltd., comprising government’s 30.48 per cen equity shareholding and LIC’s 30.24 per cent. Sarma described this as a ‘pittance.’LIC equity holding is funded by its millions of policyholders. In fairness to them, the government and LIC ought to have displayed a greater sense of prudence before parting with a 60.72 per cent equity holding at such a low price, Sarma said.

data.title: Jio’s $3.2 billion IPO tests Ambani appeal with young Indians
data.description:
For generations of Indians, Reliance Industries Ltd. was their introduction to the stock market. Founder Dhirubhai Ambani drew middle-income savers into shares, building a following that endured for decades.

Nearly fifty years after Reliance went public, his billionaire son Mukesh and grandson Akash are preparing to list the group’s telecom and digital services arm in what is set to be India’s biggest initial public offering. Jio Platforms Ltd. plans to raise about $3.2 billion in the offering, which opens on Oct. 21. The IPO will test how much the Reliance brand still matters to retail investors.

Jio is pitching to a very different market from the one Dhirubhai knew. India now has more than 130 million registered stock-market investors, nearly 40 per cent of them under 30, according to National Stock Exchange of India data. Thousands of stocks, a vast array of mutual funds and other assets compete for their money. Older shareholders regarded Reliance as a stock they could hold for decades. For younger investors, growth, profits and valuation play a bigger role in the investment decision.

Mahendra Chheda, 69, started as a floor trader in the late 1960s before becoming a member of the Bombay Stock Exchange.

“Be it Dhirubhai’s ambition, his quest to create an army of retail investors or the return of capital to shareholders, Reliance set itself miles apart,” he said. His son, Hardik, 44, an equities trader, takes a different view of Jio.

“I will be taking out profit soon after listing,” he said. “Retail investors owe a lot to the Ambanis for popularizing direct stock ownership, but we are now in a different era of financial markets.”

Reliance, under Mukesh’s leadership, has grown from a maker of textiles and chemicals into India’s most valuable company with businesses spanning energy, consumer goods and telecom.

Under Dhirubhai, a first-generation entrepreneur who challenged Mumbai’s entrenched industrial establishment, the company decided to tap thousands of individual investors to help set up his textile empire.

The November 1977 IPO raised ₹2.8 crore and drew about 58,000 investors, with the offering subscribed seven times, according to Reliance’s annual report. It helped fuel what became known as India’s ‘equity cult,’ as more households began buying shares directly. Annual shareholder meetings grew into mass gatherings, including one held at Cooperage Football Ground in south Mumbai in the mid-1980s.

Reliance shares have delivered an annualized average return of about 29 per cent since listing, according to a presentation at a Mumbai roadshow on Thursday. This year, however, the stock has fallen 23 per cent amid a broader selloff in local equities, putting it on track for its worst annual performance since 2011.

Akash, Jio Platforms’ 34-year-old managing director and Mukesh’s eldest son, is leading the company’s listing, his first major Reliance transaction on his own.

Jio had previously been expected to seek a valuation of about ₹11 lakh crore ($116 billion), people familiar with the matter have said. During global roadshows, fund managers questioned why Jio deserved a premium over smaller rival Bharti Airtel Ltd. and how it planned to make money from digital services beyond its core telecom business, Bloomberg reported.

Jio has drawn more than $20 billion in bids, and overseas investors including Fidelity Management & Research, Allianz SE and Capital Group have indicated interest, people familiar with the matter have said.

Even with that demand, Jio will sell shares at ₹1,065 to ₹1,119 apiece, valuing the company at about $108 billion at the top of the range. That puts it at a discount to Bharti Airtel’s $125 billion market value.

Prathamesh Gokhale, 24, said Jio’s growth outlook and valuation matter more to him than the Ambani legacy. He plans to bid for the IPO.

“If I get lucky with an allotment, I will sell half of my holding in the short term for a quick profit and keep the rest for longer-term gains,” he said. He also views Bharti Airtel as an attractive investment.

Gokhale, who is studying accountancy, said limited capital makes it crucial to free up money for other investments.

His approach is common among India IPO investors. A study by the market regulator in 2024 found that retail investors sold 40 per cent of their allotment within a week of listing. When returns topped 20 per cent, they disposed about two-thirds.

They also have more places to put that money. India’s $5 trillion market now includes consumer-tech firms, digital payment companies, and stock exchanges, alongside industrial groups and multinational names that once dominated trading.

Jio disrupted India’s telecom market when it entered a decade ago with cheap 4G data services. The question now is whether it can keep innovating and deliver the next leg of growth, according to Geetanjali Kedia, an investment adviser at SPTulsian.com.

“Investors have become much more discerning,” she said. “Companies need to consistently deliver returns to get their attention and money.”
